'''Melvyn Charles Usselman''' (1944–2015) was a professor of [[chemistry]] at the [[University of Western Ontario]] (UWO), with a particular focus on the history of chemistry.

==Life and career==
He studied for his BSc, MA and PhD at UWO. He married Trixie Sennema. They had four children, Jasper, Charlotte, Richard and David.<ref name="Obituary">{{cite web|url=http://yourlifemoments.ca/sitepages/obituary.asp?oId=872220|title=Melvyn Charles Usselman|website=yourlifemoments.ca|access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref>

He spent over 30 years researching eighteenth and nineteenth-century chemistry to write a biography of the English polymath and discoverer of the elements [[palladium]] and [[rhodium]], [[William Hyde Wollaston]], entitled ''Pure Intelligence: The Life of William Hyde Wollaston''. In doing this as a professional chemist and a dedicated biographer, Usselman attempted to reproduce Wollaston's experiments from the original notes, even going so far as to assay the actual samples that Wollaston had produced which were held by [[Michael Faraday]].

In a similar vein, earlier publications and experiments of his concern the work of other chemists in their golden age of discovery, including the Frenchmen [[Jacques Étienne Bérard]] and [[Claude Louis Berthollet]], the Englishmen [[John Dalton]], [[Thomas Thomson (chemist)|Thomas Thomson]] and [[Smithson Tennant]], and the German [[Justus von Liebig]].<ref name="faculty">{{cite web|title=Mel Usselman|last=Usselman|first=Mel|url=http://www.uwo.ca}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Isis: A journal of the History of Science Society|last=Levitt|first=Theresa|doi=10.1086/688432}}</ref>

In 1994-5 he won the Edward G.Pleva Award for Excellence in Teaching.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uwo.ca/tsc/awards_and_grants/excellence_teaching_awards/edward_award.html|title=Western Teaching Support Centre|website=www.uwo.ca|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref> In 1996 he won an Ontario Confederation of University Faculty Association (OCUFA) Teaching and Academic Librarianship Award.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uwo.ca/tsc/awards_and_grants/external_awards/ocufa.html|title=Ontario Confederation of University Faculty Association (OCUFA) Teaching and Academic Librarianship Awards|website=www.uwo.ca|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref> He received the [[:de:Liebig-Wöhler-Freundschaftspreis]] in 2003 for his chemical history research. He was awarded a 2004-5 University Students' Council (USC) Teaching Excellence Award
<ref>{{cite web|url=http://westernusc.ca/teaching_awards/|title=Teaching Awards|website=westernusc.ca|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref> and the USC President's Medal for Innovation in Undergraduate Teaching in 2005.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uwo.ca/tsc/awards_and_grants/excellence_teaching_awards/usc_award.html|title=University Students' Council Teaching Awards|website=www.uwo.ca|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref> He was on the USC Honour Roll five years running from 1997 to 1998.<ref name="faculty"/>

He won a posthumous award in 2016, the [[Roy G. Neville Prize]] in Bibliography or Biography for his biography of Wollaston.<ref name="Neville">{{cite web|title=Roy G. Neville Prize in Bibliography or Biography |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/roy-g-neville-prize|website=[[Science History Institute]]|date=5 July 2016 |accessdate=23 March 2018}}</ref>

He died at [[Strathroy-Caradoc|Strathroy]], Ontario on 23 March 2015 aged 70.<ref name="Obituary"/>
